10: version: 0.1.1.0
11: ---
12: 
13: # mcp-notion
14: 
15: > Notion is a cloud workspace with no headless CLI and no plugin ecosystem. This skill makes it safe to drive from an agent: the official Notion MCP for every CRUD operation, direct Notion REST API calls for the five gaps the MCP leaves open, and a knowledge layer for Notion's relational and computed model.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
20: 
21: | Aspect | What you get |
22: |---|---|
23: | **Use it for** | Notion page, block, data-source, comment, user and search operations through the official MCP, plus file uploads, views, non-truncated property items, async-task polling and daily-note conventions through direct API calls |
24: | **Invoke with** | "notion", "notion mcp", "notion workspace", "notion database", "notion page" or auto-routing on Notion keywords |
25: | **Works on** | Any Notion workspace shared with an internal integration; the local stdio MCP server via `NOTION_TOKEN` for headless and Code Mode work, the remote OAuth MCP for interactive sessions |
26: | **Produces** | Created and updated pages, filtered data-source queries, appended blocks, comments and gap operations through one MCP path and one direct-API path |
27: 
28: ---
29: 
30: ## 2. OVERVIEW
31: 
32: ### Why This Skill Exists
33: 
34: Notion is cloud-only. There is no headless filesystem to edit, no third-party plugin ecosystem to wrap, and no daily-driver CLI equivalent to ClickUp's `cupt`. The official Notion MCP covers every CRUD operation across pages, blocks, data sources, comments and users in 24 tools, but it leaves five capabilities unexposed and it does nothing to protect an agent from Notion's relational and computed model. A blind property write against a mismatched schema fails validation, and a burst of calls trips the 3-requests-per-second rate limit. A thin transport cannot fill the five gaps or route between Notion's two server backends, and Notion's lack of a plugin layer makes a full file-layer skill unnecessary. So this skill is a light workflow mode: the MCP for what it covers, direct API calls for what it does not, and a knowledge layer so both paths write correct data.
35: 
36: ### What It Does
37: 
38: This skill drives Notion through two complementary paths. The official Notion MCP handles all CRUD through Code Mode: page create, retrieve, update, archive, move and markdown round-trip; block read, append, update and delete; data-source query, retrieve, update and create; comments, users and search. Direct Notion REST API calls fill the five capabilities the MCP does not expose. An operation-based routing rule picks the path for the work at hand, and a knowledge layer supplies the hierarchy, property-type and relational semantics that keep every write valid. A page create never bypasses the schema. A file upload never fails because the MCP has no tool for it.
39: 
40: The MCP transport is owned by `mcp-code-mode`. This skill consumes Code Mode as a provider. It does not implement the transport. For the generated application code that integrates Notion, `sk-code` owns the standards and tests.
41: 
42: ### When To Use This Skill
43: 
44: Reach for this skill when you need to create, read, update or organize Notion pages, blocks, data sources, comments or users from an agent. Reach for the official MCP path for any CRUD operation in its six domains. Reach for the direct API path when the work is a file upload, a view operation, a non-truncated property read or an async-task poll. Reach for the knowledge-layer references before authoring any property, relation, rollup or formula write.
45: 
46: ### The Notion Operation Layer
47: 
48: | Capability | What the skill knows how to operate |
49: |---|---|
50: | **Pages and blocks** | create, retrieve, update, archive and move pages, append, update and delete blocks, and round-trip page content as Markdown through the official MCP |
51: | **Databases and data sources** | query, retrieve, update and create data sources under the API 2.0 data-source model, and read database metadata for data-source IDs |
52: | **Relational and computed model** | operate 22 property types, single and dual relations, rollups (14 functions) and Formulas 2.0 (about 50 functions) with correct schema, value, filter and sort semantics |
53: | **Tooling gaps** | perform file uploads, view operations, non-truncated property-item reads and async-task polling through direct Notion REST API calls |
54: 
55: ---
56: 
57: ## 3. QUICK START
58: 
59: **Step 1: Provide the integration token.**
60: 
61: The Code Mode registration already exists. The `notion` manual is defined in `.utcp_config.json` (stdio, `npx -y @notionhq/notion-mcp-server`, `NOTION_TOKEN` from `${notion_NOTION_TOKEN}`), and `.env.example` carries the `notion_NOTION_TOKEN=` line. Create an internal integration in Notion, copy its token (it starts with `ntn_`), and set it in `.env`:
62: 
63: ```bash
64: # .env
65: notion_NOTION_TOKEN=ntn_YOUR_INTEGRATION_TOKEN_HERE
66: ```
67: 
68: **Step 2: Share the pages and databases the integration needs.**
69: 
70: An internal integration sees only what is explicitly shared with it. In Notion, open each page or database, use the connection menu and add your integration. A page that is not shared returns HTTP 403, not an empty result.
71: 
72: **Step 3: Call through Code Mode.**
73: 
74: Code Mode servers are configured in `.utcp_config.json`, not `opencode.json` (that file is for native, non-Code-Mode MCP tools). The Notion manual is `notion`, launched over stdio and authenticated with the `NOTION_TOKEN` env var, so run operations inside `call_tool_chain({ code })`:
75: 
76: ```typescript
77: call_tool_chain({
78:   code: `
79:     // Tool naming follows notion.notion_{tool_name}. The underlying MCP tool ids are
80:     // hyphenated (retrieve-a-page, create-a-page, query-data-source, ...). Confirm the
81:     // exact callable form with list_tools()/tool_info() before calling — never guess.
82:     const me = await notion.notion_retrieve_bot_user({})
83:     return me
84:   `
85: })
86: // Expected: the bot user identity for your integration (confirms the token works)
87: ```
88: 
89: The local stdio server runs headless with `NOTION_TOKEN`, which is why Code Mode uses it. The remote OAuth server at `mcp.notion.com` cannot run headless. Restart your AI client after editing `.env`.
90: 
91: ---
92: 
93: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
94: 
95: ### The Operation Router
96: 
97: The skill reads your request, scores it against weighted intent signals and loads only the reference files relevant to the chosen path. A keyword such as "page", "block", "query" or "comment" routes to an official MCP tool. A keyword such as "upload", "view", "property item" or "task status" routes to a direct API gap call. A schema, relation, rollup or formula question loads the knowledge-layer references before any write. If the token is missing or the backend is unclear, the router loads the install guide first.
98: 
99: ### The Official MCP Path
100: 
101: The official server is `@notionhq/notion-mcp-server` (v2.5.1, 24 tools), registered through Code Mode: `.utcp_config.json` defines the `notion` manual, launched over stdio via `npx -y @notionhq/notion-mcp-server` and authenticated with the `NOTION_TOKEN` env var. The 24 tools span six domains: pages (7), blocks (5), databases and data sources (6), comments (2), users (3) and search (1). You reach them through Code Mode with `call_tool_chain({ code: "..." })`. The callable form follows `notion.notion_{tool_name}`, but the underlying tool ids are hyphenated (`retrieve-a-page`, `create-a-page`, `query-data-source`), so always confirm the exact name with `list_tools()`/`tool_info()` before calling. Do not guess it from the tool's description.
102: 
103: Notion API 2.0 migrated to **data sources** as the primary abstraction that replaced "databases": query a data source with `query-data-source`, not a removed database-query tool. Most tools pin API version `2025-09-03`; the two markdown round-trip tools (`retrieve-page-markdown`, `update-page-markdown`) require `2026-03-11`. The server sources the `Notion-Version` header per operation, so a mixed workflow does not need a single global version.
104: 
105: ### The Direct API Path
106: 
107: Five capabilities are not exposed by the MCP and are filled with direct Notion REST API calls: **file uploads** (five upload endpoints), **views** (view create, update, delete and query), **non-truncated page property items** (`GET /v1/pages/{page_id}/properties/{property_id}` for values the page object truncates), **async-task polling** (for long-running operations such as duplicate-page) and **daily notes** (a knowledge-layer convention, not a single endpoint). These calls use the same `Authorization: Bearer {token}` header and a `Notion-Version` header, and they obey the same rate limit as the MCP path.
108: 
109: ### The Knowledge Layer
110: 
111: Operating Notion safely means encoding its model. Three pillars: the **database to data-source to page hierarchy**; the **22 property types** with their schema, value, filter and sort semantics; and the **relational and computed model** of single and dual relations, rollups (14 functions) and Formulas 2.0 (about 50 functions). Read the knowledge-layer references before authoring a property write, a relation or a rollup, so the write passes Notion's server-side validation the first time.
112: 
113: ### Dual-Backend Routing
114: 
115: Notion ships two MCP backends, and the mode routes between them by runtime context.
116: 
117: | Backend | Transport and auth | Headless | Use when |
118: |---|---|---|---|
119: | **Local stdio** (deprecated) | `npx @notionhq/notion-mcp-server`, `NOTION_TOKEN` bearer token | Yes | Headless work and Code Mode |
120: | **Remote** (recommended) | `mcp.notion.com`, OAuth 2.0 with PKCE | No, interactive only | Interactive sessions with a browser |
121: 
122: Code Mode uses the local stdio server, because the remote OAuth server cannot complete its browser authorization step in a headless context. The local server is deprecated but still functional; treat that as a known risk to plan a migration around, not a wrong choice for headless automation.
123: 
124: ### Agent Safety Invariants
125: 
126: - Always share a page or database with the integration before operating on it. An unshared target returns HTTP 403, and a missing share is the single most common cause of "not found" confusion.
127: - Always respect the rate limit: about 3 requests per second per integration, with bursts allowed.
128: - On HTTP 429 (`rate_limited`) or 529 (`service_overload`), honor the `Retry-After` header and back off with jitter; centralize retries in the HTTP layer, not per tool.
129: - Always let the server pin the API version per operation, and never hardcode a single version across markdown and non-markdown tools.
130: - Treat tokens as opaque strings; do not validate them with a regex.
131: - Never auto-modify `opencode.json`, the Code Mode config lives in `.utcp_config.json`.
132: - Confirm every tool name with `tool_info()`; never guess it.
133: - An empty `search` result is valid and common, do not fabricate pages.
134: 
135: ### Preflight Check
136: 
137: Start every Notion session by confirming the token resolves and the integration is authenticated.
138: 
139: ```typescript
140: call_tool_chain({
141:   code: `
142:     const me = await notion.notion_retrieve_bot_user({})
143:     return me   // Expected: bot user identity — the token and connection work
144:   `
145: })
146: ```
147: 
148: ---
149: 
150: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
151: 
152: The MCP path and the direct API path cover different operation sets by design. Neither is a drop-in for the other. For "create a page" or "query this database with a filter", the official MCP is the right answer. For "upload this file to a page" or "read the full multi-select values that got truncated", only a direct API call will work.
153: 
154: This skill uses only Notion's official MCP server (`@notionhq/notion-mcp-server`, launched over stdio). It never reaches for a community MCP server. The MCP transport and the `call_tool_chain()` invocation are owned by `mcp-code-mode`. This skill orchestrates the Notion surface. It does not implement the transport.
155: 
156: ### Related Skills
157: 
158: | Skill | Relationship |
159: |---|---|
160: | `mcp-code-mode` | Owns the MCP transport. This skill consumes Code Mode as a provider and calls Notion tools through `call_tool_chain()`. |
161: | `sk-code` | Owns application-code standards and tests. This skill operates on Notion data that sk-code may produce or consume. |
162: | `mcp-click-up` | Structural sibling. Both skills own a light workflow orchestrator with operation-based routing; Notion is MCP-only with no CLI, where ClickUp adds the `cupt` CLI. |
163: | `mcp-obsidian` | Migration counterpart. This skill's knowledge layer reads a live Notion workspace's structure to drive a Notion-to-Obsidian import. |
164: 
165: ---
166: 
167: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
168: 
169: | What you see | Why | Fix |
170: |---|---|---|
171: | HTTP 401 `unauthorized` | Token missing, wrong or revoked | Re-copy the `ntn_` token from Notion settings and set `notion_NOTION_TOKEN` in `.env` |
172: | HTTP 403 on a real page | The page is not shared with the integration | Open the page, use the connection menu and add the integration |
173: | HTTP 404 `object_not_found` | Wrong ID, or the object is not shared with the integration | Verify the page or database ID and confirm it is shared |
174: | HTTP 429 `rate_limited` | Over the ~3 requests/second per-integration limit | Honor the `Retry-After` header and back off with jitter |
175: | HTTP 529 `service_overload` | Notion is overloaded | Retry with the same backoff as a 429 |
176: | HTTP 400 `validation_error` | Property schema or formula value is invalid | Read the data-source schema first; check property types and formula syntax |
177: | MCP: connection refused | `notion` manual missing, or `npx` / `NOTION_TOKEN` unavailable | Fix the manual in `.utcp_config.json`, verify `npx -y @notionhq/notion-mcp-server`, set `notion_NOTION_TOKEN` |
178: | MCP: tool not found | Wrong tool name, or version drift | Confirm with `list_tools()`/`tool_info()`; the callable form is `notion.notion_{tool_name}` |
179: 
180: ---
181: 
182: ## 7. FAQ
183: 
184: **Q: Is there a Notion CLI like ClickUp's `cupt`?**
185: 
186: A: No. Notion is cloud-only with no headless filesystem and no daily-driver CLI equivalent, so this mode is MCP-only. Every operation runs through the official MCP over Code Mode, with direct Notion REST API calls filling the five gaps the MCP does not expose. That is the deliberate difference from `mcp-click-up`, which adds the `cupt` CLI for daily task operations.
187: 
188: **Q: Local stdio server or remote OAuth server: which do I use?**
189: 
190: A: Use the local stdio server for headless and Code Mode work; it authenticates with a static `NOTION_TOKEN` and needs no browser. Use the remote OAuth server at `mcp.notion.com` for interactive sessions where a human can complete the OAuth flow. Code Mode runs headless, so it uses the local server. The local server is deprecated but still functional: plan a migration to remote for interactive use, and keep local for automation until a headless remote path exists.
191: 
192: **Q: My page or database returns 403 or "not found" even though it exists. Why?**
193: 
194: A: An internal integration sees only what is explicitly shared with it. Open the page or database in Notion, use the connection menu and add your integration. Sharing a parent page does not always cascade: share the specific object the call targets.
195: 
196: **Q: My `search` came back empty. Is that an error?**
197: 
198: A: No. An empty `search` result is valid, and `search` matches titles only, not full page content. Before you escalate, confirm the target is shared with the integration and that you are searching a title fragment. If the object is genuinely absent from the shared set, report it clearly and do not fabricate pages.
199: 
200: **Q: Which Notion API version does the mode use?**
201: 
202: A: Most tools pin `2025-09-03`, the version that introduced data sources. The two markdown round-trip tools require `2026-03-11`. The local server sources the `Notion-Version` header per operation, so you do not set one global version, let the server pin it.
203: 
204: ---
205:

2: title: README Template and Selection Guide
3: description: Concise guidance for project, skill, feature and component README files, with routing to the code-folder README template when developer topology is the main need.
4: trigger_phrases:
5:   - "readme selection guide"
6:   - "project readme template"
7:   - "skill readme routing"
8:   - "narrative readme structure"
9: importance_tier: normal
10: contextType: general
11: version: 1.2.1.0
12: ---
13: 
14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143: 
144: ```yaml
145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.
155: 
156: ---
157: 
158: ## 6. FILLABLE SCAFFOLD
159: 
160: Copy this scaffold, then remove sections that do not apply.
161: 
162: ````markdown
163: ---
164: title: "[PROJECT_OR_FEATURE_NAME]"
165: description: "[One-sentence description]"
166: trigger_phrases:
167:   - "[search phrase]"
168: version: 1.0.0.0
169: ---
170: 
171: # [PROJECT_OR_FEATURE_NAME]
172: 
173: > [One-sentence purpose statement.]
174: 
175: ---
176: 
177: ## 1. OVERVIEW
178: 
179: [Explain what this is, who it is for and why it exists.]
180: 
181: ### Key Statistics
182: 
183: | Metric | Value |
184: |---|---|
185: | Status | [Current state] |
186: | Version | [Version or release channel] |
187: | Main audience | [Who uses this] |
188: | Operating modes | [Mode count or short list] |
189: 
190: ### How This Compares
191: 
192: | Capability | This Project | Related Option |
193: |---|---|---|
194: | [Capability] | [Current behavior] | [Difference] |
195: 
196: 
197: ---
198: 
199: ## 2. QUICK START
200: 
201: ```bash
202: # Install or prepare
203: [command]
204: 
205: # Verify
206: [command]
207: ```
208: 
209: Expected result: [what success looks like].
210: 
211: 
212: ---
213: 
214: ## 3. FEATURES
215: 
216: ### Key Features
217: 
218: | Feature | What It Does |
219: |---|---|
220: | [Feature] | [Current behavior] |
221: 
222: 
223: ---
224: 
225: ## 4. REQUIREMENTS
226: 
227: | Requirement | Minimum | Notes |
228: |---|---|---|
229: | [Runtime or tool] | [Version] | [Why it is needed] |
230: 
231: 
232: ---
233: 
234: ## 5. STRUCTURE
235: 
236: ```text
237: [root]/
238: +-- [path]/        # [Purpose]
239: `-- [file]         # [Purpose]
240: ```
241: 
242: | Path | Purpose |
243: |---|---|
244: | `[path]` | [Role] |
245: 
246: <!-- For items needing more than one line, use the itemized pattern
247:      from Section 4 instead of this table. -->
248: 
249: 
250: ---
251: 
252: ## 6. CONFIGURATION
253: 
254: | Option | Default | Purpose |
255: |---|---|---|
256: | `[OPTION]` | `[value]` | [What it controls] |
257: 
258: 
259: ---
260: 
261: ## 7. USAGE EXAMPLES
262: 
263: ```bash
264: [command]
265: ```
266: 
267: Result: [expected output or behavior].
268: 
269: 
270: ---
271: 
272: ## 8. TROUBLESHOOTING
273: 
274: | What You See | Cause | Fix |
275: |---|---|---|
276: | [Symptom] | [Cause] | [Action] |
277: 
278: 
279: ---

290: ## 10. RELATED RESOURCES

292: ### Related Skills

304: ````

13: 
14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143: 
144: ```yaml
145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.
155: 
156: ---
157: 
158: ## 6. FILLABLE SCAFFOLD
159: 
160: Copy this scaffold, then remove sections that do not apply.
161: 
162: ````markdown
163: ---
164: title: "[PROJECT_OR_FEATURE_NAME]"
165: description: "[One-sentence description]"
166: trigger_phrases:
167:   - "[search phrase]"
168: version: 1.0.0.0
169: ---
170: 
171: # [PROJECT_OR_FEATURE_NAME]
172: 
173: > [One-sentence purpose statement.]
174: 
175: ---
176: 
177: ## 1. OVERVIEW
178: 
179: [Explain what this is, who it is for and why it exists.]
180: 
181: ### Key Statistics
182: 
183: | Metric | Value |
184: |---|---|
185: | Status | [Current state] |
186: | Version | [Version or release channel] |
187: | Main audience | [Who uses this] |
188: | Operating modes | [Mode count or short list] |
189: 
190: ### How This Compares
191: 
192: | Capability | This Project | Related Option |
193: |---|---|---|
194: | [Capability] | [Current behavior] | [Difference] |
195: 
196: 
197: ---
198: 
199: ## 2. QUICK START
200: 
201: ```bash
202: # Install or prepare
203: [command]
204: 
205: # Verify
206: [command]
207: ```
208: 
209: Expected result: [what success looks like].
210: 
211: 
212: ---
213: 
214: ## 3. FEATURES
215: 
216: ### Key Features
217: 
218: | Feature | What It Does |
219: |---|---|
220: | [Feature] | [Current behavior] |
221: 
222: 
223: ---
224: 
225: ## 4. REQUIREMENTS
226: 
227: | Requirement | Minimum | Notes |
228: |---|---|---|
229: | [Runtime or tool] | [Version] | [Why it is needed] |
230: 
231: 
232: ---
233: 
234: ## 5. STRUCTURE
235: 
236: ```text
237: [root]/
238: +-- [path]/        # [Purpose]
239: `-- [file]         # [Purpose]
240: ```
241: 
242: | Path | Purpose |
243: |---|---|
244: | `[path]` | [Role] |
245: 
246: <!-- For items needing more than one line, use the itemized pattern
247:      from Section 4 instead of this table. -->
248: 
249: 
250: ---
251: 
252: ## 6. CONFIGURATION
253: 
254: | Option | Default | Purpose |
255: |---|---|---|
256: | `[OPTION]` | `[value]` | [What it controls] |
257: 
258: 
259: ---
260: 
261: ## 7. USAGE EXAMPLES
262: 
263: ```bash
264: [command]
265: ```
266: 
267: Result: [expected output or behavior].
268: 
269: 
270: ---
271: 
272: ## 8. TROUBLESHOOTING
273: 
274: | What You See | Cause | Fix |
275: |---|---|---|
276: | [Symptom] | [Cause] | [Action] |
277: 
278: 
279: ---
280: 
281: ## 9. FAQ
282: 
283: **Q: [Question readers ask often]?**
284: 
285: A: [Short answer with a link when useful.]
286: 
287: 
288: ---
289: 
290: ## 10. RELATED RESOURCES
291: 
292: ### Related Skills
293: 
294: | Skill | Relationship | Use When |
295: |---|---|---|
296: | [`[skill-name]`](../skill-name/SKILL.md) | [Sibling or dependency] | [When to use it] |
297: 
298: ### Related Documents
299: 
300: | Document | Purpose |
301: |---|---|
302: | [`[Document]`](./path/to/doc.md) | [Why it matters] |
303: 
304: ````
305: 
306: ---
307: 
308: ## 7. VALIDATION CHECKLIST
309: 
310: - [ ] README type is correct. Code folders use `readme-code-template.md`.
311: - [ ] Included sections match the audience and task.
312: - [ ] No empty sections remain.
313: - [ ] Commands were tested or marked as examples.
314: - [ ] Links use correct relative paths.
315: - [ ] Frontmatter is valid if present.
316: - [ ] No Table of Contents and no `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments.
317: - [ ] HVR passes: no em dashes, semicolons, banned words or setup phrases.
318: 
319: ---
320:

# mcp-click-up Skill

ClickUp task management via **cupt CLI** (primary) and **official ClickUp MCP** (secondary). Operation-based routing: cupt handles daily task ops, and the MCP handles task creation, documents, search, lists and folders, task relations, chat and reminders. Goals, bulk create, webhooks and checklist edits have no route on either surface.

---

## 0. MARKDOWN FORMATTING CONTRACT — READ BEFORE ANY CLICKUP WRITE

ClickUp shows plain text literally. Markdown sent through a plain-text path shows up in the ClickUp UI as raw `### Heading`, `**bold**`, and `- [ ]` text. Whenever the content contains ANY markdown syntax, use the markdown-aware parameter for the operation. On the Code Mode manual (`clickup_official`), checked against the server's schema on 2026-10-08:

| Operation | Required parameter |
| --- | --- |
| Task create or update | `markdown_description` (the server has no plain `description` or `markdown_content` parameter) |
| Document page create, update or read | `content_format: "text/md"` |
| Task read-back | `include: ["description"]` on `clickup_get_task` |

On the raw ClickUp v2 REST API, `markdown_content` is also accepted on task update and `include_markdown_description=true` returns markdown, both live-verified 2026-07-15. The claude.ai ClickUp connector was not re-checked on 2026-10-08.

**Failure symptom:** literal `###` or `**` visible in a ClickUp task means someone used the plain `description` field. That is the defect, not a rendering bug.

17: # Notion Migration Inventory Reference
18: 
19: The `mcp-notion` mode's read-side method for inventorying a Notion workspace before it migrates to Obsidian. This is the read half of the migration: it produces the ledger that the `mcp-obsidian` write-side method (`references/notion-migration.md` in the `mcp-obsidian` mode, sibling in this skill package) consumes at every step. Run this inventory before the Obsidian Importer, and re-run its verification-relevant steps after.
20: 
21: ---
22: 
23: ## 1. OVERVIEW
24: 
25: ### Purpose
26: 
27: Produce the ledger the Obsidian write-side method consumes, so nothing the importer drops or truncates goes unrecorded.
28: 
29: ### When to Use
30: 
31: - Building a migration ledger before a Notion-to-Obsidian import.
32: - Reading Notion data that the standard MCP tools truncate or omit (wide relations, saved views, file uploads).
33: - Scoping a large workspace migration under the ~3 req/s rate-limit budget.
34: - Verifying inventoried data (row counts, comment threads, relation values) against a migrated Obsidian vault.
35: 
36: A migration inventory has to see more than the official MCP surface exposes. The 24-tool Notion MCP (`references/mcp-tools.md`) covers page, block, data-source, comment, user, and search CRUD, but truncates large relation/people/rich_text values at 25 references, only title-searches, and has no tool for file uploads, saved views, or non-truncated property reads. A complete inventory therefore interleaves MCP calls with the 5 direct-API gap reads in `references/api-gap-tools.md`, walking every data source, view, comment thread, and attachment before the importer ever runs.
37: 
38: ---
39: 
40: ## 2. THE 7-STEP INVENTORY PROCEDURE
41: 
42: | Step | Action | Tool / call | Produces |
43: |---|---|---|---|
44: | 1 | `search` on title roots | MCP `search` (title-only) | Top-level pages and databases to walk from |
45: | 2 | Resolve the data-source model | MCP `retrieve-a-database` → data-source ids; `retrieve-a-data-source` → full schema | Schema per data source (properties, types, relations) |
46: | 3 | Pull every row | MCP `query-data-source`, paginated | The complete row set per data source |
47: | 4 | List saved views | API gap — `GET /v1/databases/{id}/views` | Every secondary view the importer will drop |
48: | 5 | List file uploads | API gap — `GET /v1/file_uploads` | An attachment ledger to reconcile against the imported vault |
49: | 6 | Inventory comment threads | MCP `list-comments` + `list-all-users` | Full comment-thread inventory with author mapping, for reconstruction |
50: | 7 | Read non-truncated relations | API gap — `GET /v1/pages/{id}/properties/{prop}` | Complete relation/people/rich_text values past the 25-reference limit |
51: 
52: Run steps 2-3 per database before moving to the next; steps 4-7 can run in parallel once the data-source ids from step 2 are known, subject to the rate-limit budget in section 4.
53: 
54: ### Recovery routing — inventoried feature → Obsidian plugin
55: 
56: Each item this inventory surfaces maps to a specific reconstruction plugin on the Obsidian side. This is a routing summary so the inventory flags what every dropped or at-risk feature will need after the import; the recipes themselves live in the write-side method (`../../mcp-obsidian/references/notion-migration.md` §4), which since mcp-obsidian v0.24.0.0 defers plugin-specific detail to each plugin's own documentation. Route from this table — do not build from it.
57: 
58: | Inventoried feature | Obsidian recovery | Where the recipe lives |
59: |---|---|---|
60: | Relations & rollups (steps 2, 7) | Notion Bases plugin, with Dataview as a supplement for aggregations it can't express | `notion-migration.md` §4 |
61: | Saved views (step 4) | Notion Bases view configs (board / gallery / timeline / chart), with a Core-Bases / Dataview fallback | `notion-migration.md` §4 view recovery |
62: | Calendar view (step 4) | The Notion Bases calendar recipe (calendar view + Meta Bind date entry + optional Dataview agenda) | The Notion Bases plugin's own documentation; `mcp-obsidian` no longer carries the recipe |
63: | Interactive elements (buttons, date widgets) | Meta Bind + JS Engine reconstruction | `notion-migration.md` §4 interactive-element recovery |
64: | Formulas (step 2) | Notion Bases formulas, or a hand-translated static value where no Obsidian equivalent exists | `notion-migration.md` §4 |
65: | Comments (step 6) | `[!comment]` callout reconstruction | `notion-migration.md` §5 |
66: 
67: The importer drops secondary views and interactive elements entirely, so those two rows are always reconstruction, never verification. Relations, rollups, and formulas are partly auto-converted — verify first, then supplement.
68: 
69: ---
70: 
71: ## 3. THE 5 API-GAP READS USED FOR MIGRATION
72: 
73: All five gaps come from `references/api-gap-tools.md`; this table maps each to why the migration inventory needs it. Full endpoints, request/response shapes, and `Notion-Version` pinning live there — this is a routing summary, not a duplicate recipe set.
74: 
75: | Gap | Endpoint | Why the inventory needs it |
76: |---|---|---|
77: | File uploads | `GET /v1/file_uploads` | Builds the attachment ledger the post-import verification (step 8 of `notion-migration.md`) reconciles against the vault |
78: | Saved views | `GET /v1/databases/{id}/views` | The importer only converts the default table view; this is the only way to see what will be dropped and needs manual reconstruction |
79: | Property-item non-truncation | `GET /v1/pages/{id}/properties/{prop}` | `retrieve-a-page` truncates relation/people/rich_text at 25 references; a wide relation column needs this to inventory completely |
80: | Async-task polling | `GET /v1/async_tasks/{task_id}` | Needed only if the inventory itself triggers an async Notion operation (e.g. a duplication) on the local stdio backend |
81: | Daily notes | No endpoint — a knowledge-layer convention | Daily-note databases are inventoried like any other data source (steps 2-3); there is no separate gap call |
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ## 4. READ-LIMIT CONSTRAINTS
86: 
87: These four constraints shape how the inventory must be sequenced and paced — designing around them up front avoids silent data loss during the read pass, not just during the eventual import.
88: 
89: - **25-reference truncation.** `retrieve-a-page` and `retrieve-a-database` truncate `relation`, `people`, and `rich_text` values at 25 items. Any property that might exceed 25 references must be read through the property-item API gap (section 3), not the standard page/database tools.
90: - **Title-only search.** MCP `search` matches titles only — it cannot search page content. Start the inventory from the workspace tree (step 1), not from a content search; a database or page with no title match is otherwise invisible to the inventory.
91: - **`data_source_id`, not `database_id`.** API 2.0 replaced "databases" with "data sources"; queries, schema reads, and property reads all target a data-source id. Using a database id where a data-source id is required is the most common 400 during inventory.
92: - **~3 requests/second rate limit.** Per-integration throughput is roughly 3 req/s. A large workspace (50 databases, 200 data sources, 5000 pages) needs on the order of 11,500 calls for a full deep inventory — about 64 minutes at the rate limit — versus roughly 500 calls (~3 minutes) for a schema-only quick inventory. Run the quick inventory first to scope the migration, then deep-inventory only the databases that must preserve full parity.
93: 
94: ---
95: 
96: ## 5. RELATED RESOURCES
97: 
98: - `../../mcp-obsidian/references/notion-migration.md` — the write-side counterpart: the 8-step reconstruction method this inventory feeds, the recovery matrix, comment reconstruction, and the verification protocol.
99: - `references/api-gap-tools.md` — full request/response recipes for the 5 API-gap reads in section 3.
100: - `references/mcp-tools.md` — the 24-tool MCP catalog steps 1-3 and 6 of this procedure use.
101: - `references/database-model.md` — the data-source hierarchy and relation/rollup model that step 2's schema read depends on.
102: - `references/troubleshooting.md` — rate-limit backoff, `data_source_id` vs `database_id` recovery, and version-mismatch recipes.

158: Three entries need explicit handling so an agent does not treat them like ordinary columns:
159: 
160: - **`verification`** — a real page-property **value** type (confirmed on `page-property-values`), used by Notion **wiki** verification. It reports `state` (verified / unverified / expired), a `verified_by` user, and an optional `date` range. It is **read-only** and is **not** a schema-configurable column type — it does not appear in the `property-schema-object` create/update type set. Read it; never try to write it or add it to a schema.
161: - **`place`** — appears in the `property-object` schema type list but is documented as **not fully supported**. Treat its config and value shapes as `VERIFY` (confirm current support against the `property-object` reference before relying on it); do not depend on it in generated schemas.
162: - **`button`** — a Notion UI property that triggers actions. It has **no API representation**: it is not in `property-schema-object` (cannot be created via the API) and not in `page-property-values` (no readable value). If a workspace column is a button, the API simply will not expose it as a settable/gettable property. `VERIFY` only if a future API version adds it.
163:

It reports `state` (verified / unverified / expired), a `verified_by` user, and an optional `date` range. It is **read-only** and is **not** a schema-configurable column type — it does not appear in the `property-schema-object` create/update type set. Read it; never try to write it or add it to a schema.

162: - **`button`** — a Notion UI property that triggers actions. It has **no API representation**: it is not in `property-schema-object` (cannot be created via the API) and not in `page-property-values` (no readable value). If a workspace column is a button, the API simply will not expose it as a settable/gettable property. `VERIFY` only if a future API version adds it.

`notion_retrieve-a-database` calls `GET /v1/databases/{database_id}` under API version `2025-09-03`. 16: # mcp-notion API Gap Tools Reference
17: 
18: Direct Notion REST API calls that fill the 5 capability gaps the official Notion MCP server does not cover. The MCP server (`@notionhq/notion-mcp-server`, 24 tools) covers all page, block, data-source, comment, user, and search CRUD. It exposes no tools for file uploads, views, page property items, or async task polling, and Notion has no daily-notes concept at all. These five are tooling gaps: the REST API has the endpoints (except daily notes), the MCP just does not surface them, so the mode calls the API directly.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: ### Purpose
25: 
26: Turn each uncovered capability into a working direct call: the exact endpoint, method, version pin and a runnable example, with every body shape that is not fully confirmed marked VERIFY.
27: 
28: ### When to Use
29: 
30: - Attaching an image, PDF or file to a page, block, cover/icon or `files` property.
31: - Creating, editing or running a saved database view.
32: - Reading a `relation`, long `rich_text`/`title` or wide `people` field past the 25-item truncation.
33: - Polling a long-running operation on the local stdio backend.
34: - Any journaling or daily-log workflow.
35: 
36: Each section below gives the exact endpoint(s) and method, a runnable example, and when to reach for it. Two invocation styles appear throughout:
37: 
38: - **curl** — a direct shell call, the canonical form. The bearer token is always read from the environment variable `$notion_NOTION_TOKEN`; it is never hardcoded.
39: - **Code Mode** — the same HTTP call issued from inside `call_tool_chain({ code: "..." })` via `fetch()`, reading the token from `process.env.notion_NOTION_TOKEN`. Use this when the mode is already running through Code Mode and outbound HTTPS is permitted in the sandbox; otherwise fall back to a `curl` shell call through Bash.
40: 
41: All requests target base URL `https://api.notion.com/v1` and carry two headers: `Authorization: Bearer $notion_NOTION_TOKEN` and a `Notion-Version` header. Version is per-endpoint, not global — see each section and §8.
42: 
43: Endpoint paths below were confirmed against the live Notion API reference on 2026-08-21 (`developers.notion.com/reference/*` and the API index at `developers.notion.com/llms.txt`); confirmation notes are inline. Request-body schemas that could not be fully confirmed from a dedicated reference page are marked `VERIFY`.
44: 
45: ---
46: 
47: ## 2. PREREQUISITES
48: 
49: - `notion_NOTION_TOKEN` set in the environment available to the mode (an internal-connection token or PAT, prefix `ntn_` or legacy `secret_`).
50: - The target page or data source is explicitly shared with the integration/connection — direct API calls inherit the same sharing model as the MCP server. An unshared object returns 404 or 403.
51: - Rate budget: an integration averages ~3 requests/second. Batch loops (multi-part uploads, paginated property reads) must space requests and honor `Retry-After`. See §8 and `troubleshooting.md §5`.
52: 
53: ---
54: 
55: ## 3. GAP 1 — FILE UPLOADS
56: 
57: The MCP has no file-upload tool. The REST API exposes five endpoints. Uploading is a create-then-send flow; the returned `file_upload` id is then attached to a block, page cover/icon, or a `files` property.
58:

15: # Notion Database Model Reference
16: 
17: **Scope:** the structural and relational/computed model of a Notion database — how containers, tables, and rows nest; how the API 2.0 data-sources migration reshaped every query; how relations link tables; how rollups aggregate across them; and how Formulas 2.0 compute per-row values. Per-column property shapes live in `property-types.md`; this doc is the layer above them.
18: 
19: **API baseline:** Notion API version `2025-09-03`, the version that introduced data sources as the primary abstraction. The MCP server that operates this model is `@notionhq/notion-mcp-server` (see `mcp-tools.md`); several reads in this doc that the MCP truncates are completed with direct API calls (see `api-gap-tools.md`).
20: 
21: **Verification status (2026-08-21):** the hierarchy, the `database_id` → `data_source_id` migration, the relation config shapes, and the 14-function rollup config enum were confirmed against the live Notion API reference (`data-source`, `property-schema-object`, `property-object`, `retrieve-a-page-property`). Formula function families were confirmed against Notion's formula help plus widely-cited third-party references; the full ~50-function list is summarized by family below and marked `VERIFY` where an exact count matters — confirm against `notion.com/help/formula-syntax`.
22: 
23: ---
24: 
25: ## 1. OVERVIEW
26: 
27: ### Purpose
28: 
29: Keep every schema read, query and write on the right object: the data source rather than the database, a relation target shared with the integration, a rollup function the read side can compute, and a formula that validates on save.
30: 
31: ### When to Use
32: 
33: - Resolving a `database_id` to the `data_source_id` a schema read, query or row create needs.
34: - Choosing `single_property` or `dual_property` for a new relation, or setting a relation value on a row.
35: - Configuring a rollup, or interpreting the function a rollup reports on read.
36: - Writing, debugging or validating a Formulas 2.0 expression.
37: 
38: A Notion "database" is not a single flat table. As of API `2025-09-03` it is a three-level nesting:
39: 
40: ```
41: Database (container)
42:   └── Data Source (a table with its own property schema)
43:         └── Page (a row / item in that data source)
44:               └── Page Property Values (must conform to the data source schema)
45: ```
46: 
47: The consequence for an agent is concrete: **you query and write against a data source, not a database.** A database is a shell that holds one or more data sources; the schema, the rows, the filters, and the sorts all belong to a data source. Get the `data_source_id` first, then operate.
48: 
49: Three capabilities make this model more than a spreadsheet, and they are the heart of the knowledge layer:
50: 
51: - **Relations** link rows in one data source to rows in another (§5).
52: - **Rollups** aggregate a related data source's values back into a row (§6).
53: - **Formulas** compute a per-row value from other properties (§7).
54: 
55: ---
56: 
57: ## 2. THE DATABASE → DATA SOURCE → PAGE HIERARCHY
58: 
59: - **Database** — the container. `retrieve-a-database` returns its metadata **including the list of data source IDs** it holds.
60: - **Data source** — one table of data with its own `properties` schema. `retrieve-a-data-source` returns that schema; `query-data-source` returns its rows with filters and sorts.

67: 
68: ---
69: 
70: ## 4. AUTH AND SHARING FAILURES (401 / 403)
71: 
72: ### 401 Unauthorized
73: 
74: **Symptom:** any call returns 401, error code `unauthorized`.
75: 
76: **Causes:** token missing from the environment, mistyped, revoked, or from the wrong workspace. Note the token format changed on 2024-09-25 from `secret_` to `ntn_`; both still work — treat tokens as opaque and do not regex-validate them.
77: 
78: The remote MCP backend does NOT accept these tokens — it uses interactive OAuth. A token that works against `api.notion.com` and the local server will still 401 against `https://mcp.notion.com/mcp`. See §8.
79: 
80: **Fix:**
81: ```bash
82: # Confirm the variable is exported to the mode's environment
83: env | grep -c notion_NOTION_TOKEN     # expect 1
84: 
85: # Re-copy the token: Notion → Settings → Connections → your integration → Internal Integration Secret
86: # Then re-set notion_NOTION_TOKEN and re-run Quick Diagnostics step 2.
87: ```
88: 
89: ---
90: 
91: ### 403 Forbidden (or 404 on an object you can see in the UI)
92: 
93: **Symptom:** the object exists in Notion but the API returns 403, or 404 as if it did not exist.
94: 
95: **Root cause:** the page or data source is not shared with the integration. Notion scopes an internal connection to only the objects explicitly shared with it — being able to see something in the browser does not grant the token access.
96: 
97: **Fix:** in Notion, open the page/database → top-right `•••` menu → `Connections` → add your integration. Sharing a parent shares its children. Re-run Quick Diagnostics step 3; it should return 200.
98: 
99: ---
100: 
101: ## 5. RATE LIMIT 429 (BACKOFF PLUS JITTER)
102: 
103: **Symptom:** HTTP 429 (`rate_limited`) with a `Retry-After` header, or HTTP 529 (`service_overload`).
104: 
105: **Root cause:** an integration averages ~3 requests/second. Batch loops — multi-part uploads, paginated property reads, bulk page writes — blow through it. 529 is transient server overload and is handled identically.
106: 
107: **Fix — respect `Retry-After`, then back off with jitter:**
108: 
109: Doctrine for the mode:
110: 1. Centralize retries in the HTTP layer, not per-call.
111: 2. On 429/529, honor `Retry-After` (integer seconds) first; if absent, exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, ...) with random jitter.
112: 3. Space steady-state batch calls to ~333 ms apart to stay under 3 req/s.
113: 4. Cap retries; after the cap, surface the failure rather than hammering the API.
114: 
115: ```bash
116: # Single-call pattern: read Retry-After and wait exactly that long before one retry
117: resp=$(curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null "https://api.notion.com/v1/users/me" \
118:   -H "Authorization: Bearer $notion_NOTION_TOKEN" -H "Notion-Version: 2025-09-03")
119: retry=$(printf '%s' "$resp" | awk 'tolower($1)=="retry-after:"{print $2+0}')
120: [ -n "$retry" ] && sleep "$retry"
121: ```
122: There is no published way to raise the 3 req/s limit for a standard integration — design batches around it.
123: 
124: ---
125: 
126: ## 6. API-VERSION MISMATCH (400)
127: 
128: **Symptom:** a request with a valid-looking body returns 400 `validation_error`, or a newer field is silently ignored / rejected.
129: 
130: **Root cause:** the `Notion-Version` header is wrong for that endpoint. The surface is versioned per-endpoint: core CRUD pins `2025-09-03`, while file uploads, views, and async tasks require `2026-03-11`. Sending the older version to a newer endpoint (or vice versa) fails validation.
131: 
132: **Fix:** match the version to the endpoint (see `api-gap-tools.md §8`):
133: 
134: | Operation | Notion-Version |
135: |---|---|
136: | Page / block / data-source / comment / user / search CRUD | `2025-09-03` |
137: | File uploads | `2026-03-11` (required) |
138: | Views | `2026-03-11` |
139: | Async tasks | `2026-03-11` |
140: 
141: For the local MCP server, the pinned version is set via its launch env (e.g. `OPENAPI_MCP_VERSION` / `NOTION_VERSION`) in `.utcp_config.json`; direct API calls set the header themselves.
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 7. DATA-SOURCE-VS-DATABASE CONFUSION
146: 
147: **Symptom:** a call that worked against an older Notion integration now 400s or 404s; an id that looks like a database id is rejected; a "database" query returns nothing.
148: 
149: **Root cause:** Notion API 2.0 migrated the primary abstraction from **databases** to **data sources**. A database is now a container that holds one or more data sources; queries, schema, and rows live on the data source, not the database. Older code that queried a "database id" is now passing the wrong id kind.
150: 
151: **Fix:**
152: - Retrieve the database to find its data source(s), then target the **data-source id** for queries and schema (`query-data-source`, not a legacy database query).
153: - Views (`api-gap-tools.md §4`) and property reads operate on the data source. The `parent` for a new view uses `data_source_id`.
154: - When an id is rejected, confirm whether the endpoint expects a `database_id` or a `data_source_id` — they are distinct and not interchangeable.
155: 
156: This is a model change, not a bug: there is no "fix" beyond passing the correct id kind for the endpoint.
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: ## 8. LOCAL-SERVER DEPRECATION AND REMOTE-MCP MIGRATION
161: 
162: **Situation:** the open-source local stdio server (`@notionhq/notion-mcp-server`) is deprecated and no longer actively maintained; Notion prioritizes the remote MCP at `https://mcp.notion.com/mcp`. The mode uses the local server on purpose — it is the only backend that runs headless.
163: 
164: | Dimension | Local stdio (deprecated) | Remote MCP (recommended) |
165: |---|---|---|
166: | Transport / auth | stdio, `NOTION_TOKEN` bearer | Streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.0 + PKCE |
167: | Headless? | Yes — token, no browser | No — interactive OAuth only |
168: | Tool names | `create-a-page`, `retrieve-a-page`, ... | `notion-create-pages`, ... (+ async tasks) |
169: | Permissions | only explicitly shared objects | the authorizing user's full access |
170: 
171: **Migration path:**
172: - Headless / Code Mode / CI → stay on the local stdio server with `notion_NOTION_TOKEN`. Accept the deprecation risk; it is the only headless option.
173: - Interactive session with a browser → prefer the remote MCP: complete its OAuth flow (its tokens are separate — a local `ntn_` token will NOT authenticate the remote server), and use its native tool names. Async task polling (`api-gap-tools.md §6`) is built in there, so that gap disappears.
174: - If the local server is sunset before a headless remote path exists, the direct REST API calls in `api-gap-tools.md` remain the fallback for the whole surface, since they only need the bearer token.
175: 
176: ---
177: 
178: ## 9. MCP MANUAL NOT FOUND
179: 
180: ### `notion` tools not found / `list_tools()` returns zero notion entries
181: 
182: **Diagnosis:**
183: ```bash
184: # Confirm the notion manual is in Code Mode's config (not opencode.json / .mcp.json)
185: grep -A8 '"notion"' .utcp_config.json
186: # Expect: command "npx", args ["-y", "@notionhq/notion-mcp-server"], env NOTION_TOKEN
187: ```
188: 
189: **Fix:**
190: 1. Add/repair the `notion` manual under `manual_call_templates` in `.utcp_config.json`, with `NOTION_TOKEN` mapped from `notion_NOTION_TOKEN` and the `Notion-Version` env pinned.
191: 2. Ensure Node.js 18+ and `npx` are available — the manual launches the server on demand.
192: 3. Reconnect Code Mode and re-run `list_tools()`; ~24 `notion_*` tools should appear. There is no browser step for the local server.
193: 
194: ### MCP tool call returns "tool not found"
195: 
196: **Cause:** wrong callable name, or the tool does not exist on this server version (local and remote use different naming — see §8).
197: 
198: **Fix:** run `tool_info()` / `list_tools()` to confirm the exact name before hardcoding it. Do not guess; tool names differ between the local and remote backends and can change across server versions.
199:

3: description: "Reference for the official Notion MCP server (@notionhq/notion-mcp-server v2.5.1): the 24-tool catalog across 6 API domains, priority table, Code Mode invocation pattern, and the 5 uncovered domains that route to direct API calls."

16: # Official Notion MCP Tools Reference
17: 
18: - **MCP Server:** `notion` manual — the `@notionhq/notion-mcp-server` package (v2.5.1, published 2026-08-04) launched over stdio via `npx -y @notionhq/notion-mcp-server`, registered as a Code Mode manual in `.utcp_config.json`. This is the local open-source server, not the hosted `https://mcp.notion.com/mcp` OAuth server; the dual-backend split is documented in `../mcp-servers/notion-mcp/README.md`.
19: - **Auth:** `NOTION_TOKEN` environment variable (an internal integration token, prefix `ntn_`), interpolated into `.utcp_config.json`. Not OAuth — there is no browser authorization step on the local stdio backend.
20: - **Invocation:** Code Mode `call_tool_chain({ code: "..." })` via `mcp__code_mode__call_tool_chain` — a single TypeScript code string with direct access to registered tools as hierarchical functions, not an array of `{tool, input}` records.
21: - **Tool naming:** Code Mode namespaces every registered tool as `<manual_name>.<manual_name>_<tool_name>`. For this manual the pattern is `notion.notion_<tool_name>`. Notion tool names contain hyphens (e.g. `create-a-page`), which are not valid JavaScript dot-identifiers — see the invocation note in Section 8 about hyphen handling. Do not guess a tool name or its exact callable form — confirm each with `tool_info()`/`list_tools()` before calling.
22: 
23: > **Verification status (2026-08-21):** the 24 tool names below were confirmed verbatim against the official README (`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/makenotion/notion-mcp-server/main/README.md`, fetched 2026-08-21). The `notion` manual is NOT yet registered in this environment — `NOTION_TOKEN` is unset and `list_tools()` returns zero `notion.*` entries — so no name here has been live-reconfirmed through Code Mode. Treat the tool set as source-confirmed but not runtime-confirmed: re-run `list_tools()` / `tool_info("notion.notion_<name>")` once the manual is registered before hardcoding any callable. The README's prose still states "Total tools now: 22 (was 19 in v1.x)" — that count predates the two markdown tools (`retrieve-page-markdown`, `update-page-markdown`) added in a later minor release; the actual tools table lists 24, matching a third-party benchmark that counted "24 tools (one per endpoint)".
24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## 1. OVERVIEW
28: 
29: ### Purpose
30: 
31: The official Notion MCP server exposes **24 tools across 6 API domains** — one tool per Notion REST endpoint, generated from the Notion OpenAPI spec. It mutates the Notion workspace (creates pages, manages data sources, appends content), so mcp-notion is a light **workflow** mode, not a read-only transport.
32: 
33: The 6 covered domains are: **Pages (7), Blocks (5), Databases / Data Sources (6), Comments (2), Users (3), Search (1)**.
34: 
35: ### When to Use
36: 
37: Use this reference when:
38: - Routing a Notion request to a specific MCP tool (see the priority table in Section 6 and the operation table in `../ROUTER.md` section 3).
39: - Writing Code Mode `call_tool_chain({ code: "..." })` invocations against the `notion` manual.
40: - Confirming whether a capability is covered by the MCP or falls into one of the 5 uncovered domains that require direct API calls (Section 7 → `api-gap-tools.md`).
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 2. PREREQUISITES
45: 
46: - Code Mode MCP configured, with the `notion` manual in `.utcp_config.json` (not `opencode.json`, `.mcp.json`, or `claude_desktop_config.json` — those hold native, non-Code-Mode MCP tools).
47: - `NOTION_TOKEN` set in the environment Code Mode runs in — an internal integration token (prefix `ntn_`) created in the Notion integrations dashboard, with the target pages/databases shared to that integration.
48: - AI client restarted after the config change.
49: - Node.js 18+ and `npx` available (the manual launches `@notionhq/notion-mcp-server` on demand via `npx -y`).
50: 
51: See the mode `INSTALL-GUIDE.md` and `../mcp-servers/notion-mcp/README.md` for the dual-backend (local stdio vs remote OAuth) configuration.
52: 
53: ---
54: 
55: ## 3. AUTHENTICATION
56: 
57: `NOTION_TOKEN` (an internal integration token, prefix `ntn_`) is interpolated into `.utcp_config.json` for the `notion` manual. Not OAuth — the local stdio backend has no browser authorization step. Each integration only sees pages and databases that have been explicitly shared with it in the Notion UI; a `restricted_resource` / 404 usually means the page was never shared with the integration, not that it does not exist.
58: 
59: The remote backend (`https://mcp.notion.com/mcp`) uses OAuth instead and is interactive-only — see the server README for when to route to it.

16: # Official Notion MCP Tools Reference
17: 
18: - **MCP Server:** `notion` manual — the `@notionhq/notion-mcp-server` package (v2.5.1, published 2026-08-04) launched over stdio via `npx -y @notionhq/notion-mcp-server`, registered as a Code Mode manual in `.utcp_config.json`. This is the local open-source server, not the hosted `https://mcp.notion.com/mcp` OAuth server; the dual-backend split is documented in `../mcp-servers/notion-mcp/README.md`.
19: - **Auth:** `NOTION_TOKEN` environment variable (an internal integration token, prefix `ntn_`), interpolated into `.utcp_config.json`. Not OAuth — there is no browser authorization step on the local stdio backend.
20: - **Invocation:** Code Mode `call_tool_chain({ code: "..." })` via `mcp__code_mode__call_tool_chain` — a single TypeScript code string with direct access to registered tools as hierarchical functions, not an array of `{tool, input}` records.
21: - **Tool naming:** Code Mode namespaces every registered tool as `<manual_name>.<manual_name>_<tool_name>`. For this manual the pattern is `notion.notion_<tool_name>`. Notion tool names contain hyphens (e.g. `create-a-page`), which are not valid JavaScript dot-identifiers — see the invocation note in Section 8 about hyphen handling. Do not guess a tool name or its exact callable form — confirm each with `tool_info()`/`list_tools()` before calling.
22: 
23: > **Verification status (2026-08-21):** the 24 tool names below were confirmed verbatim against the official README (`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/makenotion/notion-mcp-server/main/README.md`, fetched 2026-08-21). The `notion` manual is NOT yet registered in this environment — `NOTION_TOKEN` is unset and `list_tools()` returns zero `notion.*` entries — so no name here has been live-reconfirmed through Code Mode. Treat the tool set as source-confirmed but not runtime-confirmed: re-run `list_tools()` / `tool_info("notion.notion_<name>")` once the manual is registered before hardcoding any callable. The README's prose still states "Total tools now: 22 (was 19 in v1.x)" — that count predates the two markdown tools (`retrieve-page-markdown`, `update-page-markdown`) added in a later minor release; the actual tools table lists 24, matching a third-party benchmark that counted "24 tools (one per endpoint)".
24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## 1. OVERVIEW
28: 
29: ### Purpose
30: 
31: The official Notion MCP server exposes **24 tools across 6 API domains** — one tool per Notion REST endpoint, generated from the Notion OpenAPI spec. It mutates the Notion workspace (creates pages, manages data sources, appends content), so mcp-notion is a light **workflow** mode, not a read-only transport.
32: 
33: The 6 covered domains are: **Pages (7), Blocks (5), Databases / Data Sources (6), Comments (2), Users (3), Search (1)**.
34: 
35: ### When to Use
36: 
37: Use this reference when:
38: - Routing a Notion request to a specific MCP tool (see the priority table in Section 6 and the operation table in `../ROUTER.md` section 3).
39: - Writing Code Mode `call_tool_chain({ code: "..." })` invocations against the `notion` manual.
40: - Confirming whether a capability is covered by the MCP or falls into one of the 5 uncovered domains that require direct API calls (Section 7 → `api-gap-tools.md`).
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 2. PREREQUISITES
45: 
46: - Code Mode MCP configured, with the `notion` manual in `.utcp_config.json` (not `opencode.json`, `.mcp.json`, or `claude_desktop_config.json` — those hold native, non-Code-Mode MCP tools).
47: - `NOTION_TOKEN` set in the environment Code Mode runs in — an internal integration token (prefix `ntn_`) created in the Notion integrations dashboard, with the target pages/databases shared to that integration.
48: - AI client restarted after the config change.
49: - Node.js 18+ and `npx` available (the manual launches `@notionhq/notion-mcp-server` on demand via `npx -y`).
50: 
51: See the mode `INSTALL-GUIDE.md` and `../mcp-servers/notion-mcp/README.md` for the dual-backend (local stdio vs remote OAuth) configuration.
52: 
53: ---
54: 
55: ## 3. AUTHENTICATION
56: 
57: `NOTION_TOKEN` (an internal integration token, prefix `ntn_`) is interpolated into `.utcp_config.json` for the `notion` manual. Not OAuth — the local stdio backend has no browser authorization step. Each integration only sees pages and databases that have been explicitly shared with it in the Notion UI; a `restricted_resource` / 404 usually means the page was never shared with the integration, not that it does not exist.
58: 
59: The remote backend (`https://mcp.notion.com/mcp`) uses OAuth instead and is interactive-only — see the server README for when to route to it.

16: # mcp-notion Troubleshooting Guide
17: 
18: Diagnostic recipes for the official Notion MCP server and the direct API-gap calls in `api-gap-tools.md`. Most failures fall into five classes: authentication and sharing (401/403), rate limiting (429/529), API-version mismatch (400), the data-source-vs-database model change, and backend configuration (local deprecation, manual not found). Start with Quick Diagnostics (§3), then jump to the matching section.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: Every operation here reaches Notion over the network — there is no offline or filesystem fallback. That makes three things the usual root causes: the token, whether the target object is shared with the integration, and which `Notion-Version` the request pins. The error-code map below routes each symptom to its recipe.
25: 
26: | Symptom | HTTP | Section |
27: |---|---|---|
28: | Unauthorized / token rejected | 401 | §4 |
29: | Object exists but access denied | 403 (or 404) | §4 |
30: | Rate limited / service overloaded | 429 / 529 | §5 |
31: | Validation error on an otherwise-valid body | 400 | §6 |
32: | "database" call rejected, or wrong id type | 400 / 404 | §7 |
33: | Local server deprecated / planning remote | — | §8 |
34: | MCP tool or manual not found | — | §9 |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. PREREQUISITES
39: 
40: - `notion_NOTION_TOKEN` available to the mode (internal-connection token or PAT; prefix `ntn_`, or legacy `secret_`).

3: description: "The Notion database property-type system for mcp-notion: the ~22 property types with schema config, page-value, and filter/sort shapes, plus the read-only vs writable split."
4: trigger_phrases:

6:   - "notion property schema"

8:   - "notion rollup relation formula property"
9:   - "notion filter sort properties"
10: importance_tier: "important"
11: contextType: "implementation"
12: version: 0.1.0.0
13: ---
14: 
15: # Notion Property Types Reference
16: 
17: **Scope:** the property-type system that a Notion data source's schema is built from. This is the row-and-column knowledge layer that makes `mcp-notion` a workflow mode: to create a page, an agent must supply property values in the exact shape the data source's schema demands, and to query a data source it must know which filter conditions each type supports.
18: 
19: **API baseline:** Notion API version `2025-09-03` (the data-sources era). Property behavior is stable across recent versions; markdown round-trip tools pin `2026-03-11` but do not change the property model.
20: 
21: **Verification status (2026-08-21):** the type set, config shapes, and value shapes below were confirmed against the live Notion API reference — `property-object`, `property-schema-object`, and `page-property-values`. Points that could not be pinned to a single confirmed shape are marked `VERIFY` with the endpoint that would confirm them. Do not invent property types or filter operators; confirm a data source's real schema with `retrieve-a-data-source` before composing values.
22: 
23: ---
24: 
25: ## 1. OVERVIEW
26: 
27: ### Purpose
28: 
29: Write property values in the shape the data source schema demands and query each type with the operators it supports, so a create or update validates and a filter returns rows.
30: 
31: ### When to Use
32: 
33: - Building `create-a-page` or `update-page-properties` values for a typed property.
34: - Reading a data source's schema before a write.
35: - Choosing a filter operator or sort for `query-data-source`.
36: - Checking whether a computed type can be written at all.
37: 
38: A Notion data source (see `database-model.md`) has a `properties` object: a map of property name to a config whose `type` field is one of the types below. Each property type appears in **three different shapes**, and an agent that conflates them will send malformed requests:
39: 
40: | Shape | Where it appears | What it describes |
41: |---|---|---|
42: | **Schema config** | `properties[name]` on `create-a-data-source` / `retrieve-a-data-source` | How the column is defined (options, format, expression, relation target) |
43: | **Page value** | `properties[name]` on `create-a-page` / `update-page-properties` | The cell value for one row, conforming to the schema |
44: | **Filter / sort** | `filter` and `sorts` on `query-data-source` | Which conditions the type can be queried and ordered by |
45: 
46: Two facts govern everything else:
47: 
48: 1. **Some types are read-only / computed.** `formula`, `rollup`, `created_time`, `created_by`, `last_edited_time`, `last_edited_by`, `unique_id`, and `verification` cannot be set on page creation or update. Attempting to write them fails.
49: 2. **`title` is mandatory and singular.** Every data source has exactly one `title` property; it controls the page title and cannot be removed.
50: 
51: ---
52: 
53: ## 2. THE PROPERTY TYPE CATALOG
54: 
55: The confirmed set is **22 schema property types** (`property-object`), of which `place` is documented as not fully supported. Two additional value-level entries exist: `verification` (a read-only value type surfaced on wiki pages, not a schema-configurable column) and `button` (a UI-only property with no API representation). See §6 for those two.
